newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton seen stable in Pakistan, firming in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton seen stable in Pakistan, firming in India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to hold steady in Pakistan on a lack of demand from spinners and firm in India because of restricted arrivals from producing centres, dealers said on Friday.

In Pakistan, users were not lifting yarn because of a lack of funds and rising unsold stocks at ginneries of 1.23 million 375-lb bales, broker Nasim Usman of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
Transport and delivery problems were expected during the Moslem festival of Eid al-Adha next week, he added.
Some exporters had bought low quality cotton at 2,100 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). In the kerb market, prices ranged between 2,000 and 2,500.

One exporter said stocks of unsold cotton had piled up as exporters had not started purchases in a big way because of high prices on the domestic market and a liquidity crunch sparked by interest rates of between 20 and 24 percent.
Textile mills had already bought most of their requirements, he said.

Pakistan's customs-cleared cotton exports fell to 33,387 bales between September 1, 1996 and April 3, compared to 1.706 million in the same year-ago period, an official at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
Prices are likely to remain unchanged in the next few days, Usman said.

Indian cotton prices increased as a 10-day strike by truckers restricted arrivals from producing centres, dealers in India said.
Average and medium variety cotton prices remained steady in a narrow range. Mill buying remained slow because of the strike.

"Millers were facing a glut of fabrics and yarn due to the absence of lifting from the mills following the truckers' strike, which in turn curtailed their buying of cotton from the markets," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading dealer.
He added, "Prices of superior varieties lifted during the week amid a shortage of ready stock as most of the superior cotton from the current year's crop has already been marketed."

In spot deals, Gujarat Kalyan (medium staple) rose by 200 rupees to 13,700/14,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) while long-staple Gujarat Sankar-4 rose by 300/500 to 17,000/18,000 for the average variety and 19,000/20,000 for the superior variety.
Punjab cotton remained steady amid limited activity. Punjab saw-ginned was quoted at 1,550/1,660 rupees per maund while Bengal-deshi was steady at 900/950 rupees per maund.
Arrivals of cotton in some parts of western and northern India were also hit by unseasonal rains in the week, dealers said.

"Meanwhile export of Indian cotton yarn in the world market turned slow after the recent boom as exporters from Pakistan have entered world market with a big bang," Amarsey said."Higher competition from Pakistan may restrict exports of yarn from India, which in turn may subdue local sentiment."
